haiku-low.q1: Keys are loaded at startup, before readiness. /healthz stays not-ready until all three keys are loaded.
haiku-low.q2: It retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero. It never becomes ready, the rollout halts, and old pods keep serving live traffic.
haiku-low.q3: Every 5 minutes refresh() re-reads all three keys, so a new version is picked up without restart. If the read fails, it keeps the last good value and logs a warning.
haiku-low.q4: Key values live only in process memory. They must never appear on disk, in environment variables, or in logs. Version ids may be logged.
haiku-low.q5: The prod service identity orders-api-prod has read-only access to orders-api/prod/*. Only the security on-call may write prod secrets. Engineers get no prod read access.
haiku-low.q6: NOT STATED why deleting alone is insufficient. The doc says current keys count as leaked; rotating and revoking old keys at the provider makes the old values harmless.
haiku-low.q7: Clients call secrets.get(name) on every request instead of copying the key at construction, so a refreshed key takes effect without restart.
haiku-low.q8: It waits until every running instance reports the new version id on /healthz, for more than one refresh interval, before revoking the old key.
haiku-low.q9: Set store access, copy keys into the store, switch the app to read from the store, remove keys from the committed file, then rotate keys at the providers.
haiku-low.q10: Local runs use APP_ENV=dev and read only the dev sandbox keys in orders-api/dev/*. Engineers may read and write dev. The authentication method is NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q11: NOT STATED. The doc says /healthz stays not-ready until all three keys are loaded, but does not say whether the app exits or retries.
haiku-low.q12: NOT STATED. Security has not decided on a rotation cadence, and the plan does not pick one.

sonnet.q1: Keys are loaded first: load() reads all three at startup, and /healthz stays not-ready (non-200) until all three are loaded; only then does it return 200.
sonnet.q2: It retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and the old pods keep serving, so live traffic is unaffected (maxUnavailable: 0).
sonnet.q3: refresh() re-reads all three keys every 5 minutes, so a new version is picked up without restart. If a read fails, it keeps the last good value and logs a warning.
sonnet.q4: Held only in process memory. They must never go to disk, environment variables, or logs (version ids may be logged).
sonnet.q5: Read: only the prod service identity orders-api-prod (read-only on orders-api/prod/*); engineers get no read access to prod values. Write: only the security on-call.
sonnet.q6: The old values remain in git history and in earlier container images (the file is committed and copied into every image), so they count as leaked. Rotating to new keys and then revoking the old keys at the provider makes the old values harmless.
sonnet.q7: Provider clients call secrets.get(name) on every request instead of copying the key at construction, so they get the refreshed in-memory value.
sonnet.q8: Wait until every running instance reports the new secret version id on /healthz (which takes longer than one refresh interval); only then revoke. If any instance still reports the old version, do not revoke.
sonnet.q9: 1) Set store access; 2) create/copy keys into the store; 3) add the secrets module and switch the clients (then deploy and verify); 4) remove keys from the repo file (after prod verified); 5) rotate keys, then confirm and revoke old ones.
sonnet.q10: From the dev sandbox keys in the secret store (orders-api/dev/*), via make run with APP_ENV=dev. Sandbox keys are from each provider; engineers may read/write orders-api/dev/*. Whose identity is used to authenticate to the store is NOT STATED.
sonnet.q11: NOT STATED. (The document only says load() reads all three and /healthz stays not-ready until all three are loaded; it doesn't describe a missing secret specifically.)
sonnet.q12: NOT STATED / undecided. A regular schedule is an open question that security has not decided; the plan picks no cadence (it only does a one-time rotation because current keys count as leaked).
